title: Israeli strikes kill Gaza education official and wife, third senior Hamas figure in three days
dek: Medics said at least nine people were killed overnight across Gaza. Israel says Khaled Abu Nada ran Hamas's finances; Hamas called the killing a 'heinous crime' and a breach of the ceasefire.
author: Declaration Desk
body:
An Israeli air strike on an apartment in Deir al-Balah, in central Gaza, killed Khaled Abu Nada, a senior official in Gaza's Hamas-run education ministry, and his wife early on Thursday, according to medics at Al-Aqsa Martyrs Hospital. He was the third senior Hamas figure Israel has killed since Tuesday, after two security officials, on the third straight night of air strikes despite the ceasefire agreed in October 2025.

Medics in Gaza said at least nine Palestinians were killed overnight and on Thursday, including six in two strikes in Gaza City's Tuffah neighbourhood and the Beach (Shati) refugee camp, and a 62-year-old man shot in the Bureij camp. Reports gave slightly different totals during the day. These figures have not been independently verified.

## What each side says

Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and Defence Minister Israel Katz said Abu Nada was "a Hamas figure responsible for the group's economy and education portfolios". The Israeli military said he managed Hamas's banking and investment network and directed money towards militant activity. Netanyahu said Israel had killed about 80 Hamas militants in the past month and that "no one in the Hamas leadership will manage to evade us", according to reports.

Hamas confirmed Abu Nada's death but did not respond to Israel's account of his role. It called the targeting of academics and civilian figures a "heinous crime", said the killings breached the ceasefire and international law, and held US President Donald Trump's Board of Peace responsible for failing to stop them. Gaza's interior ministry accused Israel of trying to spread chaos; the security officials killed earlier this week were named in reports as Naim Abu Nahl, the internal security director, and Mohammed Abu al-Ouf, internal security chief for northern Gaza.

## The ceasefire, a year on

The US-backed ceasefire has reduced but not ended the fighting, and it has not achieved Hamas's disarmament, which Israel demands. Gaza's health ministry says more than 1,600 Palestinians have been killed since the truce took effect, 130 of them this month, and more than 6,000 wounded; Israel says five of its soldiers have been killed in the same period. The ministry puts the total death toll since October 2023 at 74,746. Israel rejects the ministry's figures as unreliable and denies accusations of genocide, saying it is acting in self-defence after the Hamas-led attack of 7 October 2023, in which about 1,200 people were killed in Israel.

Israeli forces now control around two-thirds of the Gaza Strip, up from a little over half when the ceasefire began, according to reports, behind a demarcation known as the Yellow Line. Hamas holds a narrow strip along the coast.

## Why it matters for India

India has backed the US-led ceasefire plan and has repeatedly called for humanitarian aid to reach Gaza and for a negotiated two-state solution. Renewed escalation in Gaza adds to pressure across a region where India has large stakes: millions of Indians work in the Gulf, and the confrontation between the US and Iran has already closed much of the Strait of Hormuz, through which a large share of India's oil and gas imports normally passes.

## What happens next

Israel says the targeted killings will continue while Hamas refuses to disarm. Aid groups have warned that winter rains threaten the makeshift shelters and tent camps where much of Gaza's population now lives, according to reports.
